ta-l1d48q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 48, the last of Book I. Having treated God's will, Lombard treats the conformity of our will to his: a bad human will may agree with God's will in the same thing willed while a good human will tends to the contrary; God's good will is sometimes fulfilled through man's bad will; and an objection is excluded. From this he solves two questions, on the passion of the head, Christ, and on the passion of the members, the martyrs, noting a difference between them. Four articles are announced: whether the human will can be conformed to the divine; in what conformity principally consists; whether all are bound to it; and whether they are bound also to conformity in the thing willed.
claims: A bad will can agree with God's in the thing willed; God's good will can be fulfilled through bad wills.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e121.summary: First argument that the human will cannot be conformed to the divine. Isa. 55:9 says 'as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways above yours', and earth can never be conformed to heaven.
claims: God's ways exceed ours.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e127.summary: Second argument. Things infinitely distant have no conformity, which implies approach, and God's will is as distant from man's as God from man (Gloss on Ps. 32).
claims: Infinite distance excludes conformity.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e133.summary: Third argument. Conformity is agreement in one form, and things agreeing in something have something prior and simpler than themselves, and nothing is simpler or prior to the divine will.
claims: Conformity needs a prior common form.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e137.summary: Fourth argument. Only the conformable is conformed, conformity being a relation of equiparance, and we do not call the divine will conformed to the human.
claims: Conformity is mutual.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e140.summary: Sed contra. Nothing regulated becomes right except by conformity to the rule, and the divine will is the rule of the human will, as his intellect of the human intellect.
claims: God's will is the rule of ours.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e143.summary: Second sed contra. The will of one who obeys voluntarily is conformed to the will of the one commanding, and many voluntarily obey divine precepts.
claims: Obedience conforms wills.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e146.summary: Thomas's determination. Conformity is agreement in one form, the same as likeness caused by unity of quality (Metaphysics 5), so something is conformed to God as assimilated to him. Things are called like either by participating one form, as two white things whiteness, so every like thing is composed of what it shares and what distinguishes it, likeness being only of different things (Boethius), and in this way nothing can be like, agreeing with, or conformed to God, as philosophers often say; or by one that has a form by participation imitating what has it essentially, as a white body might be called like separate whiteness. Such likeness, implying composition in one and simplicity in the other, can belong to a creature participating goodness or wisdom, which in God are his essence, and so our will is conformed to his. This can be understood of the power of will given to man after the exemplar of the divine will, belonging to the likeness of the image and common to good and bad, which is not the question here; or of the act of will, also called will, which is the question, since merit or demerit consists in it, man causing the act of will but not the power, so this conformity belongs only to the good.
claims: Our will is conformed to God's by imitation, not by sharing a common form.
The conformity in question is of the act of will, in which merit lies, belonging only to the good.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e149.summary: Reply to the first argument. The Lord speaks there of the wicked, signified by earth, who depart from divine likeness in their act of will.
claims: Isaiah speaks of the wicked.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e152.summary: Reply to the second argument. Between the infinitely distant there can be no conformity by equality or by agreement in something both participate, but there can be in the way described.
claims: Conformity by imitation spans infinite distance.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e156.summary: This also answers the third argument, which concerns the first mode of likeness distinguished.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. According to Dionysius, the reversal of likeness does not hold between causes and effects where likeness is by imitation, but only among equals with likeness by similar participation in the same; we do not say a man is like his image, but conversely. So God is not like or conformed to a creature, but the creature is conformed to God, imitating him as far as it can.
claims: Likeness by imitation is not reciprocal.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e171.summary: First argument that conformity of wills consists principally in the thing willed. Conformity is agreement in form, and the form and perfection of will is the thing willed, as the known is the knower's perfection.
claims: The willed is the will's form.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e174.summary: Second argument. Acts are known and judged by objects (the Philosopher), and the will's object is the thing willed.
claims: Acts are judged by objects.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e177.summary: Third argument, against conformity in the good as object. Will is only of good, so every will, even of sin, would be conformed to God's.
claims: Every will seeks good.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e181.summary: Fourth argument. The will of Christ's killers agreed with God's not only in the same thing but in a good, Christ's passion, a great good.
claims: Christ's killers willed a good.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e184.summary: Fifth argument. Goodness comes from the end, yet one acting for a good end may not be conformed to God's will, as one who steals from the rich to give alms to the poor.
claims: A good end does not suffice.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e187.summary: Sixth argument, against conformity in willing what God wills us to will. Willed and willing coincide only per accidens, when one's willing is willed by another, so our willing is conformed to God's only per accidens; so conformity should be in the thing willed.
claims: Willing what God wills us to will is accidental conformity.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e190.summary: Sed contra. Two contraries as such are not conformed to the same, yet two saints' wills of opposite things are both conformed to God's, being right, as some did not will Paul's death, which he willed.
claims: Saints can will opposites rightly.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e193.summary: Thomas's determination. The question concerns the act of will, which can imitate the divine act by its natural being, belonging to it as from the power, set aside, or by the added perfection by which it is such or such, a conformity as in moral species, which is the question. This can be considered by the four causes: material, the same thing willed, the matter of the act, which is conformity only in some respect, since being simply is from form; efficient, when one wills what God wills him to will, since God made this order of will in him; final, when one orders his deeds to God's glory, for which God does all things, and in these two conformity consists essentially; and formal, willing from charity as God wills all from charity, the form of the act being from the habit, and in this the perfection of conformity consists. The reason: essential assimilation follows that from which species is taken, and every voluntary act takes its species from its object, the form of the will producing it. In an object there is something material and something formal completing its character, as light and colour in the visible: whatever thing is willed is material, and the character of good completes it. So the human act of will is conformed to the divine by tending to good as the divine will does, representing divine goodness, which is conformity by efficient cause, since God ordered every will to good, and this God wills us to will as our will is ordered. This includes conformity of end, since the thing willed has the character of good from the end, though sometimes good in itself too, so conformity is essentially from this, not from the thing willed, from which the act does not take its species. The habit of charity adds perfection to the act's goodness, so the perfection of conformity is by formal cause, the act being more conformed the better and more perfect it is.
claims: Conformity consists essentially in willing good as ordered by God and for his glory, not in the thing willed.
It is perfected by charity, the formal cause.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e196.summary: Reply to the first argument. The thing willed is the will's perfection or object only as under the character of good, as colour is the object and perfection of sight only under the act of light.
claims: The willed is object only under the character of good.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the third argument. In a sinner the will of reason tends not to its own good but to another's, the concupiscible and irascible, and man is man by reason, not by these, so the will is not good. If the irascible tended per se to its own object, its good, it would not be culpable, as in brutes, and would have some conformity to God's will, tending to what God ordered it to.
claims: The sinner's rational will pursues the lower appetites' good, not its own.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Christ's passion had two aspects: as saving the human race, under the character of good, willed by God and the saints; and as afflicting an innocent, without the character of good, willed by the Jews, so they willed good only per accidens, and per se willed evil esteemed good, as satisfying their anger or envy.
claims: Christ's killers willed the passion as affliction, not as salvation.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. As natural form is in matter from the agent, the form of goodness is in the thing willed from the end, and as matter disproportioned to a form never receives it even with the proper agent, as stone does not become flesh by digestion, a thing willed disproportioned to goodness never receives goodness, however good the end, such as things evil in themselves, like stealing, unless the deformity is removed by divine authority (Dist. 47).
claims: A good end cannot make an intrinsically evil act good, barring divine authority.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e212.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. Everything God wills imitates his will as being as God wills, but not in the character of willing and goodness of the act of will; only the human act of will tending to the good to which it is ordered by God's will does, so the conformity of our will is not only as willed but as willing and eliciting a good act of will.
claims: Conformity is of our will as willing, not merely as willed.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e224.summary: First argument that we are not bound to conformity with the divine will. As the will's rectitude is by conformity to the divine will, the intellect's is by conformity to the divine intellect, but not all are bound to conform their intellects, or no one with a false opinion would be saved.
claims: We are not bound to conform our intellects.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e227.summary: Second argument. No one is obliged to what is impossible to him, or sin would be necessary, and a will obstinate in evil cannot be conformed to the always-good divine will.
claims: The obstinate cannot conform.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e230.summary: Third argument. Whoever sins does not conform his will in the act of sin, so if all are bound to conformity, every sinner sins doubly, by transgression and by omitting conformity, which is false.
claims: Sin would be doubled.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e234.summary: Fourth argument. Whoever omits what he is obliged to do sins mortally, and whoever sins venially does not conform his will in that act, so he would sin mortally, which is false.
claims: Venial sin would be mortal.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e237.summary: Fifth argument. Whatever God wills to happen happens, so whatever he wills us to will we will, and the wicked do not will to do good, so God does not will them to will good, and sinners depart from what they are bound to, so they are not bound to will what God wills them to will.
claims: God's will is always fulfilled.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e240.summary: Sixth argument. As God's willed thing is unknown to us, so is the end to which he orders his work, since even in nature ends are hard to assign, and no one is bound to the unknown.
claims: The divine end is unknown.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e243.summary: Seventh argument. No one is bound to what is not in his power, and having charity is not from ourselves.
claims: Charity is not in our power.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e246.summary: Sed contra. All are bound to obey God and have a right will, which requires conformity to his will.
claims: Obedience requires conformity.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e249.summary: Thomas's determination. One is properly bound to what one incurs sin by not doing. In natural and voluntary things sin occurs when something fails to reach what it is ordered to (Physics 2), as in monsters and errors of art, but differently: in natural things defect from order comes from necessity of matter, while in voluntary things the will itself causes its defect, since it is in our power to fail or not, so the will's defect has the character not only of sin but of fault. Since conformity of will consists in tending by its act to what it is ordered to, lack of conformity brings sin and fault, so we are bound to conformity. We are bound directly to what is per se in our power, the conformity by which we will what befits us to will and according to the right end, since we can do both by natural powers; indirectly to what is not in itself in our power, like having grace, though we can do something by which we will have it, and so we are bound also to the conformity by the form of charity.
claims: We are bound to conformity of will, since failing it is sin and fault.
We are bound directly to willing rightly and for the right end, indirectly to charity, by doing what disposes to grace.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e253.summary: Reply to the first argument. Will and intellect differ, since the intellect's defect is not in our power as the will's is, the intellect being sometimes compelled by arguments (Metaphysics 5) but not the will. Yet in what is necessary for salvation, matters of faith, we are bound to conform our intellect to the divine, since if we do what is in us divine help will not be lacking; and in other matters one would sin by voluntarily attacking the truth he understands and adhering to falsehood.
claims: We are bound to conform our intellect in matters of faith.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e256.summary: Reply to the second argument. While the will is obstinate it cannot be conformed, but in the wayfaring state no one cannot lay aside obstinacy and be conformed; for the damned it is inflicted as punishment that they never be cured of obstinacy, yet perpetual fault remains in them with unending punishment, though they do not demerit, not being on the way but at its end, where punishment is.
claims: In this life obstinacy can be laid aside; the damned remain in fault without demerit.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e259.summary: Reply to the third argument. Conformity of will is common to all precepts of natural and written law ordering us to good, so whoever sins against any precept sins against conformity, but does not commit two sins, since the common is not counted with the proper.
claims: Sin against conformity is not a second sin.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e262.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Affirmative precepts do not oblige always, since we cannot always act (De somno et vigilia), so we need not always actually conform our will, but always habitually and sometimes actually; so one who sins venially acts not against conformity but beside it, as beside the law.
claims: Venial sin is beside, not against, conformity.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e265.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Conformity in willing what God wills us to will concerns antecedent will, whose effect is the order of our nature to good; the objection concerns consequent will.
claims: Conformity concerns antecedent will.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e268.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. Though we cannot know the proper end, we can know the last end, from which all goodness in proximate ends comes, so as to order all things to God, who made all things for himself (Prov. 16:4).
claims: We know the last end and can order all to God.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e272.summary: The seventh argument is answered by what was said.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e285.summary: First argument that we are not bound to conformity in the thing willed. No one is bound to the unknown, and God's willed thing is unknown to us, like his foreknown.
claims: God's willed thing is unknown.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e288.summary: Second argument, against the reply that it can be revealed. If someone's damnation were revealed to him, he would not be bound to will his damnation but rather his salvation, since he is bound to love himself from charity and desire the highest good for himself.
claims: One need not will one's own damnation.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e291.summary: Third argument. Christ knew his passion was willed by God, yet by some will did not will it (III, Dist. 17), and Christ omitted nothing of right living.
claims: Christ in some will did not will his passion.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e295.summary: Fourth argument. The Blessed Virgin did not will her son's passion, or she would not have grieved, against Luke 2:35, 'a sword will pierce your own soul'.
claims: Mary grieved the passion.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e301.summary: Fifth argument. God's will is known through signs, and permission, one of them, concerns evils of fault, which we must in no way will.
claims: Permission concerns evil.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e304.summary: Sed contra. The Gloss on Ps. 100:4 says he has a perverse heart who does not will what God wills, and all are bound not to have a perverse heart.
claims: Not willing what God wills is perversity.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e313.summary: Second sed contra. Friends will and nill the same (Cicero), and we are bound to be God's friends.
claims: Friends will the same.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e316.summary: Thomas's determination. God wills some things by antecedent will, and undoubtedly we must conform our will to him in these, since this is what our will is ordered to. He wills some by consequent will, not always known to us except as manifested by his operation, and this adds a character of goodness to the thing so that it can be willed because God wills it: as almsgiving is good in itself and receives further goodness from the end, so a thing receives goodness from being willed and ordered by God, since what is apprehended as willed by God is apprehended as good, and the will following this apprehension is bound to tend to it, or its movement would not be good or conformed to God, fleeing a good. But since there are different grades of appetite following different apprehensions, no appetite is bound to tend to a good whose character it does not apprehend: sensitive appetite, following sense, is only of bodily fitting good, the sensibly pleasant, and in no way of spiritual good like knowledge; natural will, following reason considering absolutely, wills what is good for man as man, knowledge, virtue, health; and deliberate will, following reason deliberating about the end and circumstances, tends to what is good from the end or a circumstance. What has all these characters of goodness every right appetite tends to; where one is lacking, the corresponding appetite does not tend to it, perhaps to the contrary, as being cut for health is painful to sense and not good in itself but only from the end, so only deliberate will chooses it, while natural will and sensitive appetite shrink. So when something is apprehended as willed by God, especially through the sign of operation, the deliberate will, following reason weighing this character of goodness, is bound to will it, though natural will and sensitive appetite shrink, and in shrinking they are conformed to God's will, tending to good according to the character they apprehend, as one who piously grieves the death of a father or someone useful to the Church. In sinners the deliberate will is corrupted, abandoning reason's deliberation and following the impulse of natural and sensitive will, murmuring against God's ordering; in the just on the way it remains whole but imperfect, in knowledge, not fully knowing God's will, and in affection, retarded by lower movements, so it suffices not to resist divine ordering, without needing to feel joy in what happens by it, as it suffices for the brave not to be saddened in mortal danger, though not rejoicing; this is the conformity of the way. In the blessed it is whole and perfect, knowing God's will fully and with affection dominating all lower will, so they rejoice in seeing what God wills, as Ps. 57:11 says the just will rejoice when he sees vengeance.
claims: We must conform to God's antecedent will always, and to his consequent will with our deliberate will once it is known.
Natural will and sensitive appetite may rightly shrink from what God wills, as Christ's did; wayfarers need only not resist, while the blessed rejoice.
concepts: conformity of the way vs. of the homeland

ta-l1d48q1-d1e322.summary: Reply to the first argument. What God wills by antecedent will is known to us by natural inclination; what he wills by consequent will is known by revelation or operation.
claims: Antecedent will is known by nature, consequent by revelation or events.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e326.summary: Reply to the second argument. That supposition is quasi-impossible, since no one's damnation is revealed, not even to angels (Augustine); if it were, one could take it as a threat, not as foreknowledge; still one is bound to will the order of justice by which, if he dies in sin, he is damned, since this is what God wills, not damnation per se or fault.
claims: One must will the order of justice, not one's damnation.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e329.summary: Reply to the third and fourth arguments. Christ willed his passion by deliberate rational will, as did the Blessed Virgin and every saint, though natural will dissented.
claims: Christ and Mary willed the passion by deliberate will, while natural will shrank.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e332.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Permission never signifies that God's will is of fault, but of the good joined to fault.
claims: Permission signifies will of the good joined to fault.

ta-l1d48q1-d1e341.summary: An expositio textus closing Book I. (1) 'God did not will the act of the Jews' seems false, since passion is the effect of action, but Christ's passion fell under two operations: the Jews' action, as afflicting, not willed by God, any more than the action; and the operation of Christ's will, as meritorious, pleasing to God, as the verse says, 'the action displeased, the passion pleased'; will and reason often divide what nature joins. (2) Peter was called Satan, adversary (Matt. 16), as opposing Christ's good will with his own good will out of piety. (3) Lombard's order seems unfitting, since our natural way is from posterior to prior, from creatures to Creator; but this holds of natural knowledge, beginning from sense, while knowledge by faith rests on first truth itself, so we must proceed from first truth, God, to what is from him, after the likeness of the knowledge the saints will have in the Word, where they will know both the Word and things fully, a knowledge in which the Son, the Word of God, who began it in us by faith, makes us share; to him be honour and glory for ever. Amen.
claims: Christ's passion displeased God as the Jews' act and pleased him as Christ's merit.
Theology proceeds from God to creatures because faith rests on first truth, anticipating knowledge in the Word.

ta-l1d48q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 48 divides Lombard's treatment of the conformity of our will to God's, and its application to the passion of Christ and the martyrs, and announces four articles: possibility, principle, obligation, and conformity in the thing willed.
claims: Bad wills can agree with God in the thing willed.

ta-l1d48q1-Dd1e113.summary: Article 1 holds that our will can be conformed to God's by imitation, not by sharing a common form, and that the conformity in question is of the act of will, in which merit lies. Likeness by imitation spans infinite distance and is not reciprocal: the creature is like God, not God like the creature.
claims: Our will is conformed to God's by imitation.

ta-l1d48q1-Dd1e163.summary: Article 2 holds that conformity consists essentially in willing good as God ordered our will, efficiently, and for his glory, finally, and is perfected by charity as formal cause, not in agreement about the thing willed, which is merely material. Christ's killers willed the passion as affliction, a good end cannot make an intrinsically evil act good, and conformity is of our will as willing.
claims: Conformity lies in the character of good and the end, perfected by charity.

ta-l1d48q1-Dd1e216.summary: Article 3 holds that all are bound to conformity of will, since failing it is sin and fault. We are bound directly to willing rightly and for the right end, indirectly to charity, and in matters of faith to conforming our intellect. The obstinate can repent in this life, sin against conformity is not a second sin, venial sin is beside conformity, and we know the last end.
claims: We are bound to conformity of will.

ta-l1d48q1-Dd1e277.summary: Article 4 holds that we must conform to God's antecedent will always and to his consequent will, once known, with our deliberate will, while natural will and sensitive appetite may rightly shrink, as Christ's and Mary's did at the passion. Wayfarers need only not resist God's ordering, while the blessed rejoice in it. One must will the order of justice, not one's damnation, and permission concerns the good joined to fault.
claims: Deliberate will must conform to God's known will; lower appetites may rightly shrink.
concepts: conformity of the way vs. homeland

ta-l1d48q1-Dd1e336.summary: The Expositio textus closing Book I distinguishes Christ's passion as the Jews' displeasing act and Christ's pleasing merit, explains Peter as 'Satan', and justifies proceeding from God to creatures because faith rests on first truth, anticipating knowledge in the Word.
claims: Theology proceeds from God because faith rests on first truth.

ta-l1d48q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 48, which closes the book, treats the conformity of human to divine will. Article 1 holds that our will can be conformed to God's by imitation, in its act. Article 2 holds that conformity consists essentially in willing good as God ordered and for his glory, perfected by charity, not in the thing willed. Article 3 holds that all are bound to conformity, directly to right willing and indirectly to charity. Article 4 holds that the deliberate will must conform to God's known will, though natural will and sensitive appetite may rightly shrink, as Christ's did at his passion.
claims: Conformity to God's will consists in willing good as he ordered, perfected by charity.
All are bound to it; the deliberate will must accept God's known will, though lower appetites may shrink.
